name: Bukhara Arabic, dialect of the Bukhara Arabs, kishlaks Jogari and Arab-khana
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 6 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Vinnikov, I. N. 1969. Jazyk i fol'klor buxarskix arabov [Language and folklore of the Bukhara Arabs]. Moscow: Nauka, Glavnaja redakcija vostočnoj literatury. Preface (Predislovie), pp. 3-11. Parallel: Vinnikov, I. N. 1962. Slovar' dialekta buxarskix arabov. Palestinskij sbornik 10 (73), preface pp. 5-6 and s.v. -ha; Vinnikov 1949, Sovetskoe vostokovedenie 6, p. 121 n. 1.
catalog_locator: Vinnikov 1969, preface pp. 10-11 (transcription note 'Несколько слов о транскрипции') and p. 5 ('Ударение' paragraph); 1962 parallel: preface pp. 5-6, s.v. -ha p. 228, s.v. la p. 189 and s.v. ma p. 197 ('без ударения'); 1949, p. 121 n. 1
catalog_quote: Долгота гласных отмечается в двух случаях: 1) когда она совершенно отчетливо воспринимается на слух: mōt, kōl ... ilēha и т. д. и 2) когда на нее указывает ударение, сохранившее у бухарских арабов свой исконный характер: šibʿān, riǧǧāl, giddām, ibʿīr, tišrabīn, zaǧīr, ǧayīn, lakēt, šaddēt, mitmūt и т. д. В конце слова под ударением может иногда быть и краткий гласный, особенно в заимствованных словах, и когда ударение передвинуто на конец слова из-за столкновения с ударением предшествующего слова: ḥalwoyitár suwí 'сладкий кисель сделай (ж.)!' Когда в слове есть долгий гласный, ударение не отмечается, так как всегда в таком случае ударение падает на долгий гласный. Когда же в слове два долгих гласных, что вообще чрезвычайно редко, ударение отмечается. Знак между словами внизу указывает на то, что эти слова имеют одно ударение (ср. makkēf в древнееврейском); в этих случаях ударение отмечается всегда.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.translation: 2) when it is indicated by the stress, which among the Bukhara Arabs has preserved its original character: šibʿān, riǧǧāl, giddām, ibʿīr, tišrabīn, zaǧīr, ǧayīn, lakēt, šaddēt, mitmūt, etc. At the end of a word a short vowel may occasionally also be under stress, especially in loanwords, and when the stress has been shifted to the end of the word because of a clash with the stress of the preceding word: ḥalwoyitár suwí 'make (f.) sweet kisel!' When a word contains a long vowel, the stress is not marked, since in that case the stress always falls on the long vowel. When a word has two long vowels, which is altogether extremely rare, the stress is marked.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is attracted to the syllable with a long vowel (heavy syllable) wherever a word has one, and the author treats Bukhara Arabic stress as having kept its 'original' (Old Arabic, weight-based) character; the examples show stress on the long-vowel syllable whether it is final (riǧǧāl, giddām, tišrabīn, mitmūt) or non-final (kōyil, sakkīna, ilēha). A final short vowel can carry stress only in loans or under stress clash. For words without a long vowel the note gives no general rule; the only explicit remark (Vinnikov 1962 s.v. -ha, p. 229) is that in forms with the 3f.sg. suffix -ha the stress is 'always on the penult' (malbaka, matbaha, safu).
new_statements.exceptions: p. 5 ('Ударение'): the two villages differ in the imperfect of forms VII and VIII, Arab-khana stressing the second syllable (minḥásad, minḥáfar, minṭábaḥ, mirtáʿad) and Jogari the first (mínḥasad, mínḥafar, mínṭabaḥ, mírtaʿad); also Arab-khana éysab / iysáb 'where?' vs Jogari always eysáb, iysáb; Arab-khana manáh 'chin' vs Jogari mánah. Final short vowels may be stressed in loanwords and under clash with a preceding word's stress. Words with two long vowels are 'extremely rare' and get stress marked individually.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress in transcribed texts and dictionary citation forms; a tie sign marks groups of words bearing a single stress (clitic groups, compared to Hebrew maqqef), and stress can move to a word's final syllable under phrase-level clash, so some phrase-level effects are described. The remark is a transcription note, not a full phonology section.
new_statements.identity_note: The statement describes the Bukhara dialect of Central Asian (Uzbekistan) Arabic, recorded 1936-1943 in the kishlaks Jogari (Gijduvan district) and Arab-khana (Vabkent district), Bukhara oblast, Uzbekistan = Glottolog dialect buxa1234 'Buxara Arabic' under taji1248 (Glottolog 5.3 keeps Qashqa-Darya Arabic separate as uzbe1248, ISO auz; the Balkh/Afghanistan variety is balk1259, for which no stress statement was found). Vinnikov notes the two Bukhara villages differ in stress placement in some forms (Arab-khana minḥásad vs Jogari mínḥasad).

sources.note: p. 5 'Ударение' paragraph: Arab-khana vs Jogari differ in stress of VII/VIII imperfects (second vs first syllable) and a few lexemes; pp. 10-11: stress has kept its original character, always falls on a long vowel when present, final short vowel stressed only in loans/under clash; one stress per clitic group.
